visual_accuracy.rationale: Lesson 2 presents the correct variables, constraint, surface-area function, derivative, optimum, and verification consistently, while Lesson 1 relies on many generic or misleading box illustrations that often look closed/filled rather than open-top and includes several vague decorative visuals not accurately tied to the mathematics.

interactivity.rationale: Both lessons have absent gate specs and absent plan JSON, so neither provides any functional checkpoints or input-accepting questions.

narration_quality.rationale: Lesson 1 is clear, naturally paced, and mostly well-phrased with only minor wording issues, whereas Lesson 2 is heavily garbled, repetitive, fragmented, and contains unintelligible math narration defects.

sync.rationale: Both lessons provide only external-video transcripts without any visual cue offsets or beat timing, so neither can be shown to synchronize visual changes with narrated references better or worse than the other.

concept_accuracy.rationale: Lesson 1 correctly derives the volume constraint, surface area function, derivative, optimal side length, height, and minimum area in a clear pedagogical sequence, whereas Lesson 2 is largely incoherent, omits or garbles key equations and the final answer, and would not reliably help a learner understand the optimization.

polish.rationale: Lesson 1 has a cohesive, centered, clean illustrated style with readable text and few visual artifacts, while Lesson 2 looks like an unpolished screen-captured Beamer deck with persistent cursor, navigation/status bars, and garbled caption overlays cluttering the bottom of many frames.

aggregator.explanation: Lesson 1 is the clear overall winner. Three high-confidence agents favored Lesson 1: narration quality (0.99), concept accuracy (0.99), and polish (0.96), emphasizing that it is clearer, more coherent, mathematically reliable, and visually cleaner. Lesson 2 won only visual accuracy, though with high confidence (0.94), because its mathematical visuals and equations were more consistently tied to the problem. Interactivity was a high-confidence tie because neither lesson included functional checkpoints, and sync was also a tie due to lack of timing evidence. Overall, the strongest pedagogical dimensions—concept accuracy and narration—strongly favor Lesson 1, so the single Lesson 2 advantage does not outweigh them.
